content: Several studies were excluded from the analysis for various reasons. Studies with irrelevant designs, such as narrative reviews or commentaries, were excluded. Six studies were excluded because they did not include participants with visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and HIV co-infection. Additionally, six studies on secondary prophylaxis were excluded as they were conducted in ineligible settings. Six systematic reviews were also excluded, as their included studies were screened for relevance but did not yield any additional studies for inclusion. No relevant ongoing trials were identified. Efficacy and Safety (PICO 1: Treatment) Two randomized studies provided data on the efficacy and safety of combination therapy compared to monotherapy. One study was conducted in two centers in Ethiopia (2019), and the other in a single center in India (2019). Both were randomized trials designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combination therapy versus monotherapy. The Ethiopian study employed a sequential design with stopping rules and interim analyses after every 10 participants. Recruitment in the monotherapy arm was stopped after the first 10 participants reached day 29 (total n=19), while recruitment in the combination therapy arm continued until 20 participants reached day 29 (total n=39). The Indian study recruited a total of 150 participants, with 75 in each arm. Four single-arm cohort studies evaluating combination therapy were identified but not included in the review. However, a summary of their results is provided in Appendix 7. Characteristics of Included Studies for PICO 1 The Ethiopian study (2019) was conducted at the University of Gondar Teaching Hospital and the Abdurafi Health Centre. The Indian study (2019) was conducted at the Rajendra Memorial Research Institute in Patna, Bihar. Both were open-label randomized trials. The Ethiopian study used a sequential design with interim analyses, while the Indian study was a parallel-arm trial. Recruitment for the Ethiopian study occurred between August 2014 and August 2015, while the Indian study recruited participants from January 2017 to April 2018. In the Ethiopian study, 59 participants were randomized (20 in the monotherapy arm and 39 in the combination therapy arm). Participants were aged 21–51 years, with 57 males and 1 female. In the Indian study, 150 participants were randomized (75 in each arm), aged 18–64 years, with 118 males and 32 females. Diagnosis of Leishmaniasis and HIV Leishmaniasis was diagnosed through visual parasite confirmation by microscopy in tissue aspirates, with spleen aspirates preferred or bone marrow aspirates used in cases of contraindication. Patients were eligible regardless of whether it was their first episode of VL (primary case) or a relapse case with single or multiple relapses. HIV status was determined using two rapid tests, followed by a third confirmatory test in case of discrepancies. Within the trials, HIV status was reconfirmed using an enzyme immunoassay. Pregnant women were excluded from the trials, and pregnancy tests were conducted for all female participants under 50 years of age at baseline. Secondary Prophylaxis (PICO 2) One comparative retrospective cohort study from India (2017) and two non-comparative prospective cohort studies from Ethiopia (2015 and 2019b) provided data on the efficacy and safety of secondary prophylaxis. The Indian study compared monthly liposomal amphotericin B (1 mg/kg) or deoxycholate amphotericin B with no secondary prophylaxis. The Ethiopian studies assessed pentamidine as secondary prophylaxis. In the Ethiopian 2019b study, patients with CD4 cell counts ≤200/μL received pentamidine as secondary prophylaxis, while those with CD4 counts >200 did not. The characteristics of the three studies included for secondary prophylaxis outcomes are presented in Table 2. Risk of Bias and Certainty of Evidence The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach. For PICO 1 (treatment), the certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low, indicating limited confidence in the effect estimates. The main reasons for downgrading were limitations in study design (e.g., unblinded trials) and imprecision. The studies reported few events, and confidence intervals often included no effect, potential benefit, and potential harm. For PICO 2 (secondary prophylaxis), the overall certainty of evidence was very low. The main reasons for downgrading were limitations in study design (non-randomized or non-comparative studies without control groups) and lack of adjustment for confounding factors. Small sample sizes and selection bias were also detected. Outcomes All-Cause Mortality: Both Ethiopian and Indian studies reported on all-cause mortality. No significant differences were observed between treatment and control groups in either setting. Clinical Cure: Both trials reported on clinical cure rates. However, heterogeneity was observed between the studies, and no significant differences were found between treatment groups. Serious Adverse Events: Both trials reported on serious adverse events. In the Ethiopian study, 8/39 participants in the combination therapy group and 2/19 in the monotherapy group experienced serious adverse events. Detailed adverse events are reported in Appendix 8. Adverse Events: One trial (Ethiopia 2019) reported on adverse events, with low certainty evidence. Follow-Up: One trial (Ethiopia 2019) reported on patient follow-up, with low certainty evidence. Patient Satisfaction: No studies reported on patient satisfaction with the interventions. Summary of Findings The cure rate for VL-HIV patients was 65% in one setting and 95% in another. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was low to very low, indicating that the true effect may differ substantially from the estimated effect.
